g9-biology-ub2-t1.overview: What makes something alive? Not movement — a river moves. Biologists use seven shared life processes; anything running all seven is alive, and a car engine running 'energy' fails the rest.
objectives: List and explain the seven life processes (MRS GREN)
Give examples of each process in plants and animals
Contrast plants and animals on nutrition, response and movement
Apply the criteria to judge whether something is living
g9-biology-ub2-t1.simple: Memorize MRS GREN — the seven tests of life: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition. Every living thing does ALL seven. Plants do them too: they respire day and night (not just photosynthesize), respond to light, excrete oxygen and water as wastes, and reproduce. The differences: animals feed by ingesting (heterotrophs) and move freely; plants make their own food (autotrophs) with rooted, slow responses.
g9-biology-ub2-t1.detailed:
Movement in animals is active locomotion via muscles; plants show directional growth movements — phototropism (stem toward light), geotropism (roots down), and rapid nastic movements like the mimosa leaf or Venus-flytrap. Respiration is the chemical release of energy from food inside cells (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy) — distinct from breathing, which is just gas exchange; a seed respires without lungs.

Sensitivity (response to stimuli) lets organisms detect light, temperature, touch, chemicals — animals through nerves and senses, plants through growth responses to hormones. Growth is a permanent increase in size AND complexity from more/larger cells — a crystal 'grows' by adding outside layers, which is why growth alone can't define life; nutrition does the same work: a flame 'consumes' fuel but builds no cells.

Excretion is removing metabolic wastes — substances produced by the cell's own chemistry: CO₂ from respiration, urea from protein breakdown, excess water and salts. Ejecting undigested feces is egestion, NOT excretion — a classic exam trap. Plants excrete oxygen (photosynthesis waste), shed leaves full of crystals, and store tannins in bark and fallen fruit.

Reproduction passes life forward: asexually (one parent, identical offspring — bacteria splitting, potato tubers) or sexually (two parents, variation — flowers, humans). An individual may be sterile (a mule) yet its species lives — the criterion applies at species level.

Applying MRS GREN exposes near-misses: a car moves, 'eats' fuel, breathes air, releases waste, even 'grows' a dent — but it does none of these as a cell-based, self-building, reproducing system: non-living. A seed looks inert yet respires slowly and will germinate — alive, in dormancy. Viruses occupy the border: genes and proteins, but zero independent life processes — they only replicate inside a host.

Plant vs animal in one table: nutrition (photosynthesis vs ingestion), movement (growth-directional vs locomotion), response (slow-hormonal vs fast-nervous), growth (indeterminate at tips vs determinate), storage (starch vs glycogen), and the cell walls and chloroplasts only plants own (learned in the next unit).

keyTerms.def: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition
Cellular energy release from food (not breathing)
Detection of and response to stimuli
Removal of metabolic wastes (CO₂, urea, water)
Permanent increase in size and complexity by cell gain
Synonym for sensitivity in plants and simple animals

formulas.name: Aerobic respiration equation
formulas.meaning: Glucose is broken down with oxygen to release usable energy
formulas.when: Every cell, day and night — in plants and animals alike

workedExamples.problem: A student says a fallen leaf is dead because it doesn't move. Use MRS GREN to argue both sides.
workedExamples.calculation: detached leaf: no growth, no reproduction, transport cut — respiration stops within days
workedExamples.answer: It was alive on the tree (all seven processes); fallen and browning, it is dying/dead tissue — movement alone was never the test

workedExamples.problem: Which is excretion, which egestion? (a) sweating salts, (b) passing feces, (c) exhaling CO₂, (d) urinating urea.
workedExamples.answer: (a), (c), (d) are excretion (made by cells); (b) is egestion — never absorbed into cells

workedExamples.problem: A candle flame 'uses wax, gives out heat and light, gets bigger'. Alive?
workedExamples.calculation: no cells, no reproduction, no metabolism, no response, no excretion
workedExamples.answer: Non-living — it satisfies only a loose appearance of two criteria

commonMistakes: Saying plants 'don't respire' or 'only photosynthesize at night' — respiration runs 24/7
Equating movement with locomotion — plant tropisms count
Counting feces as excretory waste (it's egestion)
Growth = getting bigger: crystals and fat cells both 'grow' without being alive per se
Claiming response needs a nervous system — plants respond too
applications: Veterinary & farming: recognizing life-process failure = spotting sick livestock early
Storage science: drying grain slows respiration to keep seed alive through seasons
Gardening: phototropism explains why seedlings bend toward windows
Conservation: reproductive rates decide whether a species can recover from poaching
g9-biology-ub2-t1.summary: Seven processes define life — MRS GREN. Respiration is cellular (24/7, plants too), excretion means metabolic waste only, growth is permanent cell-based increase, and response doesn't require nerves. Plants differ from animals mainly in autotrophic nutrition and growth-based movement. Apply all seven, never one.

questions.q: The letters MRS GREN include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Excretion, not secretion, is a life process criterion.
Every cell respires; lungs only exchange gases.

questions.q: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the body?
questions.explanation: CO₂ is a metabolic waste — its removal is excretion.

questions.q: A plant bending toward a window demonstrates:
questions.explanation: Phototropism: response to light via directional growth.

options: make their own food by photosynthesis

questions.q: A crystal growing in solution fails the life test mainly because it lacks:
questions.explanation: Its growth is surface addition with no life processes behind it.

questions.q: The correct respiration word equation is:
options: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
questions.explanation: The other option is photosynthesis — the reverse.

questions.q: Distinguishing living from non-living, which single feature is LEAST reliable?
questions.explanation: Non-living things move (cars, rivers) and some living things don't (adult plants, corals).

g9-biology-ub2-t2.overview: Millions of species, one filing system: taxonomy names and groups life by shared features, from kingdom down to species, using a two-word Latin address every scientist on Earth recognizes.
objectives: Recall the hierarchy: kingdom → phylum/division → class → order → family → genus → species
Write and interpret binomial names correctly
Describe the five kingdoms and their defining features
Use simple characteristics to place an organism in a kingdom
g9-biology-ub2-t2.simple: Classification = sorting life into nested groups by shared features. The ladder: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species (think: 'Kings Play Chess On Fine Green Silk'). Every species gets a two-part Latin name — binomial nomenclature: Homo sapiens (genus capitalized, species lowercase, both italicized). Five kingdoms: Monera (bacteria — no nucleus), Protista (algae, amoeba), Fungi (mushrooms — absorb food), Plantae (photosynthesizers), Animalia (consumers, no cell walls).
g9-biology-ub2-t2.detailed:
Classification exists because there may be 10+ million species — scientists need a universal, stable filing system. Local names fail (one plant has fifty names; one name hides fifty species), so taxonomy, formalized by Carolus Linnaeus (1700s), sorts organisms into the hierarchy: Kingdom (largest group) → Phylum (animals) or Division (plants) → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species (the basic unit: organisms that interbreed to produce fertile offspring). Each step down narrows shared characteristics: all big cats share family Felidae; within it, the lion and the leopard share genus Panthera but differ at species level (P. leo vs P. pardus).

Binomial nomenclature rules: the first name is the genus (capitalized), the second the species epithet (lowercase), both italicized when typed or underlined when written; usually Latin or Greek in origin; e.g. Zea mays (maize), Escherichia coli. A well-formed name is unique worldwide — language never becomes a barrier to science.

The five kingdoms by cell type and nutrition: Monera — prokaryotes (no nucleus, bacteria, cyanobacteria), unicellular, autotrophic or heterotrophic; Protista — simple eukaryotes (amoeba, paramecium, algae), mostly unicellular, the 'catch-all' kingdom; Fungi — eukaryotes with chitin cell walls that absorb digested food externally (moulds, yeasts, mushrooms), decomposers; Plantae — multicellular eukaryotes, cellulose walls, chloroplasts, photosynthesis; Animalia — multicellular eukaryotes, no walls, ingest food, nervous and muscular systems, active movement.

Modern systems refine this: three domains (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) rest on molecular evidence — classification is hypothesis-driven, re-drawn as DNA data arrives (whales moved in with hippos!). Viruses stay outside all kingdoms: acellular, they cannot run life processes alone.

Dichotomous keys operationalize classification: paired either/or questions ('nucleus present? yes/no; chloroplasts?…') walking the user to a name. Construct them from observable traits, first to last — cell type → walls → nutrition → symmetry → specialized systems — mirroring how the kingdoms diverge.

keyTerms.def: Science of naming, describing and classifying organisms
Basic unit; interbreeding natural populations with fertile offspring
Simple eukaryotes: algae, protozoa — the informal kingdom
Fungi digest externally and absorb — decomposers
Paired-choice questions that identify an organism step by step

workedExamples.problem: Write the name 'homo sapiens' correctly and explain each part.
workedExamples.answer: Homo sapiens — genus Homo (human-like, capitalized), species epithet sapiens (wise, lowercase); italicized together

workedExamples.problem: An organism: unicellular, no nucleus, some cause disease. Which kingdom? Name another member.
Lion = Panthera leo, leopard = Panthera pardus. What does the shared first word show?
workedExamples.answer: Same genus (Panthera) — they are close relatives; the different second words mark them as different species

workedExamples.problem: First step of any dichotomous key separating Monera from the rest?
workedExamples.answer: Is genetic material enclosed in a nucleus? No → Monera; Yes → continue to other kingdoms

commonMistakes: Capitalizing BOTH words of a binomial (only the genus is)
Confusing species epithet with the species name — neither alone names a species
Placing mushrooms in Plantae (no chloroplasts — fungi absorb, don't photosynthesize)
Calling all microbes bacteria — protists and fungi are microbes too
Saying viruses 'belong to Monera' — they're outside all kingdoms (acellular)
Thinking classification is permanent — DNA data reshuffles it (three-domain system)
applications: Farmers & agronomy: correct species IDs decide which weeds, rusts or pests you're fighting
Medicine: identifying the exact pathogen selects the right drug (bacterial vs viral)
Biodiversity surveys: Ethiopian high-endemic species need names before they can be protected
Quarantine & trade: customs checks species lists — invasive brown argentine ant vs harmless ants
Forensics and food safety: DNA barcoding traces meat, honey and timber to species
g9-biology-ub2-t2.summary: Taxonomy files life into a hierarchy (KPCOFGS) and names each species with a universal binomial (Genus species, italicized). Five kingdoms sort by nucleus, walls and nutrition: Monera (prokaryote), Protista (simple eukaryote), Fungi (absorptive), Plantae (photosynthetic), Animalia (ingestive). Keys identify step-by-step; new evidence re-draws the map.

options: Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Phylum, Kingdom, Class, Order, Genus, Family, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Order, Class, Family, Species, Genus

questions.explanation: First word = genus, second = species epithet.

The basic unit of classification is the:
Why Latin names instead of local ones?
questions.explanation: One species, one name — worldwide; local names vary and clash.

questions.q: Two organisms in the same genus must also share the same:
questions.explanation: Hierarchy: same genus ⇒ same family, order, class, phylum, kingdom.

questions.q: Viruses are excluded from the five kingdoms because they:
options: are acellular and can't carry out life processes alone
questions.explanation: Not cells, no independent metabolism — outside the living filing system.
